text: Generator, brute force, comparison loop.

Stress testing (对拍) finds the bug the samples did not show. You need three programs: your solution, a slow but obviously correct brute force, and a generator of small random inputs. Run all three in a loop and stop at the first input where the two answers differ: that input is a tiny, concrete failing case.

Keep the random tests small (n ≤ 10, values ≤ 10): bugs show up just as often, and a failing case of size 5 can be traced by hand. Include edge cases on purpose: n = 1, all values equal, the maximum and minimum values.

stress.sh 1 # stress.sh (Git Bash / Linux). Windows cmd: same idea with a .bat file and fc 2 g++ -O2 -o sol sol.cpp && g++ -O2 -o brute brute.cpp && g++ -O2 -o gen gen.cpp 3 for i in $(seq 1 10000); do 4 ./gen $i > in.txt 5 ./sol < in.txt > out1.txt 6 ./brute < in.txt > out2.txt 7 if ! diff -w out1.txt out2.txt > /dev/null; then 8 echo "different on seed $i"; cat in.txt; break 9 fi 10 done

Pass the seed on the command line so a failing case can be reproduced exactly. diff -w ignores trailing spaces. When the brute force itself is wrong, both disagree with a hand-checked tiny case: check the brute on the samples first.

A generator seeded with the time produces the same test many times per second; use the loop counter as the seed. For problems with several valid answers, compare with a checker program that validates your output instead of diff.
Fast I/O, containers, memory order, contest habits.

Constant-factor optimisation (常数优化) matters when the complexity is right but the time is close to the limit. The biggest wins are almost always: fast input / output, avoiding heavy containers in inner loops, and memory access in order.

Change Why it helps Typical gain ios::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(nullptr); cin no longer syncs with C stdio 3–10× on large input "\n" instead of endl endl flushes every line large on big output custom reader with getchar (below) no format parsing 2× over fast cin array instead of map / unordered_map no hashing, no tree, cache-friendly 5–20× loop order i-k-j for matrix products reads rows in memory order 2–5× on large matrices avoid % in hot loops (compare and subtract) division is slow up to 2× vector.reserve , global arrays no repeated allocation small but free #pragma GCC optimize("O3") more compiler work (not allowed everywhere) varies
Reading 10⁶–10⁷ numbers is where input speed matters. This reader handles negative numbers and any whitespace. Do not mix it with cin on the same input.
Measure before optimising: a better algorithm beats every constant trick. Use these only when the complexity is already the intended one.

Contest habits: compile with -Wall -Wextra and read every warning; test n = 1 and the maximum sizes; check overflow (int vs long long) and array sizes before submitting; on OI-style contests, secure the subtasks with a simple method before trying the full solution.

Key points to memorise
1. 对拍 : solution + brute force + small random generator, loop until they differ.
2. Seed by loop counter; keep tests tiny; check the brute on samples.
3. Multiple valid answers: write a checker instead of diff.
4. Fast cin: sync_with_stdio(false) + cin.tie(nullptr); "\n" not endl.
5. Arrays over maps in hot loops; memory in order; avoid % in inner loops.
6. Complexity first, constants second.
